title: Rethinking GFlowNet Training: Negative Reinforce Dynamics

paper.title: Rethinking GFlowNet Training: Negative Reinforce Dynamics
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are models that learn to sample discrete
objects proportional to a target reward. They are trained by minimizing balance
errors over sampled trajectories, which inherently ties correctness to exploration: if
a region is not visited, balance cannot be enforced there. Adaptive exploration is
therefore crucial, yet standard training relies on a semi-gradient update that treats
the sampling distribution as fixed at each optimization step. On the other hand, the
full gradient
reveals a second mechanism that reduces the observed errors in an anti-exploratory
manner. In this paper, we establish a connection between the full gradient and min-min
dynamics between the GFlowNet and a decoupled sampler, showing that the sampler
reduces observed violations
by avoiding high-error regions. This insight motivates a bridge between two-player games and
single-policy dynamics, which underpins the design of our proposed method, Negative
Reinforce Dynamics (NRD).
By tying the parameters of an adversarial game together, we recover a single-policy
dynamic that extends exploration
while maintaining correctness. In standard benchmarks, our method outperforms
existing approaches in both convergence speed and exploration efficiency,
without training a separate teacher or auxiliary exploration policy.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn stochastic policies that construct structured objects with probability proportional to a nonnegative reward ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ) . Their ability to generate diverse high-reward samples has made them useful in applications ranging from biological sequence design ( Jain et al., 2022 ) and Bayesian structure learning ( Deleu et al., 2023 ) to recent approaches for language-model post-training ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Bartoldson et al., 2025 ) . Training a GFlowNet to sample from the target distribution is formulated by enforcing balance conditions, with correctness holding if and only if balance is satisfied globally ( Bengio et al., 2023 ) . During training, however, balance can only be corrected on trajectories that are observed, leaving poorly visited regions potentially uncorrected ( Madan et al., 2025 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026b ) . To mitigate this problem, training trajectories are often collected from an exploratory sampler, such as an ε \varepsilon -greedy policy, in order to broaden coverage ( Whitammer et al., 2022 ) . Previous work has furthermore introduced exploration mechanisms that use auxiliary samplers or teacher policies to expose the GFlowNet to regions where balance errors remain large ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) . In this paper we opt for a different path, revisiting how we solve the balance conditions in GFlowNet training. In the usual training pipeline, balance is enforced by turning local violations into a loss and minimizing its expectation over a sampling policy. However, with an adaptive sampling distribution that evolves during training, decreasing this expected loss may not correspond to correcting the underlying violations: if the policy adapts to avoid high-loss regions, then we will reduce the expected loss while retaining significant balance violations. This can be seen by analyzing the gradient of this expected loss, when differentiating through a parameter-dependent sampler Q θ Q_{	heta} , using the score-function identity ( Williams, 1992 ) : ∇ θ 𝔼 τ ∼ Q θ ​ [ L θ ​ ( τ ) ] = 𝔼 Q θ ​ [ ∇ θ L θ ​ ( τ ) ] ⏟ semi-gradient + 𝔼 Q θ ​ [ L θ ​ ( τ ) ​ ∇ θ ​ log ⁡ Q θ ​ ( τ ) ] ⏟ score term .

(1) This reveals two mechanisms for decreasing the loss: one which corrects balance violations (the semi-gradient term) and one which avoids high-loss regions (the score term). Standard GFlowNet training keeps only the former by using a semi-gradient , which holds the sampling distribution fixed in the gradient computation even when that distribution depends on θ 	heta . The second term reveals an additional mechanism through which the sampling distribution can reduce the expected loss, which, under ordinary minimization, lowers the objective without enforcing balance – which is generally undesirable. Nevertheless, we ask whether this mechanism can instead be turned into a beneficial exploration signal. To do so, we reframe the full-gradient dynamics encapsulated in Equation 1 as a ‘weight-tied’ version of a cooperative two-player game between the GFlowNet and the sampling policy, and argue that it is this cooperation that leads to the harmful score term. To rectify this we formulate a second game, this time adversarial , which yields a novel beneficial exploration mechanism. By appropriately tying the two players’ weights we obtain our proposed scheme, Negative Reinforce Dynamics (NRD) , which we find to perform significantly better than standard trajectory balance training, at little additional cost. We establish theoretical guarantees for these dynamics in tractable population models. In the free-trajectory setting, NRD converges globally to the balanced solution and admits a pointwise log-ratio discrepancy comparison with semi-gradient Trajectory Balance. In one-dimensional exponential families under fast normalization, NRD reaches any positive Jeffreys-divergence threshold sooner from a common initialization, with an unbounded additive advantage in the two-trajectory setting. Finally, we evaluate NRD across multimodal distribution-matching and structured-generation tasks. The method improves convergence to target distributions and finite-budget exploration relative to standard Trajectory Balance and comparable-cost baselines, while remaining competitive with approaches that train auxiliary exploration policies. Despite its two-player motivation, NRD requires only a sign-selective score correction, applied only to trajectories with negative residuals, on top of the standard Trajectory Balance update and does not require a separately trained sampler. sections.heading: 3 Rethinking GFlowNet Training
sections.text: In this section, we investigate how the score mechanism can be used to shape exploration. We first separate the GFlowNet from its sampler to make their distinct roles explicit, and then study what happens when their dynamics are tied back into a single policy. This reveals a correspondence between GFlowNet–sampler games and single-policy updates that will motivate our method in the next section.

sections.heading: 3.1 Expected Loss as a Surrogate
sections.text:

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments test whether the behavior predicted by the theory holds in practice. We ask whether NRD improves distribution learning and high-reward discovery relative to TB, and whether these gains require a separately trained exploratory policy. Comparing with alternative training losses isolates the effect of the update rule; comparing with auxiliary exploration methods tests how much exploration benefit survives when sampler and GFlowNet are tied. We evaluate both target-distribution fit and the discovery of distinct high-reward modes.

sections.heading: 6.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: For distribution learning, we use Rings, Moons, and 8 Gaussians in DiffusionGrid, adapted from the finite-horizon random-walk setting of Dall’Antonia et al. (2026b) , and the HyperGrid construction benchmark ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Whitammer et al., 2022 ) . Many paths lead to each terminal state, but finite-budget exploration can still concentrate on only part of the multimodal target. We measure estimated terminal total variation (TV) from normalized reward. For high-reward discovery, we use Bags, Knapsack128, and autoregressive sequence tasks adapted from prior structured benchmarks ( da Silva et al., 2025 ) , tracking the mean log-reward of the top 200 unique objects encountered. We also study peptide design ( Jain et al., 2022 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) , counting distinct sequences that satisfy a screening criterion from an oracle trained on GRAMPA ( Witten and Witten, 2019 ) . The first baseline group changes the training objective without adding an exploration policy. It comprises TB, the asymmetric Linex(1) loss ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , and the pairwise Contrastive Balance (CB) objective ( da Silva et al., 2024 ) . The second group explicitly trains exploratory models through ACE’s adversarial sampler ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) , SA-GFN’s novelty-seeking sibling policy ( Madan et al., 2025 ) , or Adaptive Teacher’s discrepancy-driven teacher ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . We use four seeds and the prescribed budgets. Each such step counts a policy update, including auxiliary-policy updates. Appendix A gives environment definitions, architectures, optimization settings, estimators, and the complete structured results. Appendix B provides baseline context and wall-time curves; Appendix C contains the score-distribution ablation.

Curves use the full optimizer-step budgets and report means with one-standard-deviation bands across four seeds. NRD has the lowest mean final estimated TV in each panel. Rings provides the clearest example. TB and CB remain at high error for substantial portions of training, whereas NRD keeps improving, ending at estimated TV 0.110 0.110 against TB’s 0.639 0.639 . This illustrates the gap between a loss admitting the correct distribution and its optimization reaching that distribution within a finite budget. The advantage on Rings and Moons also appears over substantial shared portions of those time axes. NRD also remains competitive with auxiliary exploration methods, including those driven by auxiliary rewards, although some sequence tasks favor ACE or Adaptive Teacher. These results extend the peptide findings to other combinatorial spaces, supporting effective high-reward discovery without a separately trained exploration policy.

sections.heading: 7 Related Work
sections.text: Approaches to improving exploration in GFlowNet training follow two main directions. The first changes the training objective while keeping a single policy; the second learns an additional mechanism that redirects sampling toward regions the GFlowNet has not yet learned. Within the first direction, Linex(1) ( Hu et al., 2025 ) replaces the squared residual with a zero-avoiding loss designed to encourage exploration and sample diversity, and f f -Trajectory Balance ( Fawkes and Hartford, 2026 ) generalizes this loss design to the family of f f -divergences. Contrastive Balance ( da Silva et al., 2024 ) compares the residuals of pairs of trajectories so that the partition function cancels. With a closely related objective, Stable-GFlowNet ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) links mode collapse to the variance of the estimated normalizer and shows that removing it yields more diverse samples. In the second direction, ACE ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) sets up a cooperative two-player game in which an exploration GFlowNet samples proportionally to the reward in regions under-allocated by the canonical GFlowNet. SA-GFN ( Madan et al., 2025 ) trains a sibling GFlowNet whose reward combines the task reward with a novelty bonus, and Adaptive Teacher ( Kim et al., 2025 ) trains a teacher GFlowNet rewarded by the student’s loss and the task reward, steering the student toward high-error regions. Boosted GFlowNets ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026b ) train a sequence of GFlowNets, each fitting the reward not yet captured by its predecessors. These methods make exploration adaptive, but at the cost of training and maintaining models beyond the principal policy, along with additional hyperparameters such as allocation thresholds and reward exponents. NRD combines features of both directions. Like the methods in the first, it trains a single policy without auxiliary models and introduces no hyperparameters beyond those of Trajectory Balance; like those in the second, it includes an explicit mechanism that directs training toward unresolved balance violations. This mechanism, however, is obtained from the policy’s own score term rather than from a separately learned sampler or teacher, and it does not arise from a choice of loss. Although we analyze and evaluate NRD with Trajectory Balance, the same construction could in principle be applied on top of other balance losses.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Negative Reinforce Dynamics, a novel GFlowNet training scheme that arises as a ‘weight-tied’ version of an adversarial game between the GFlowNet and a trajectory sampler. By selectively reinforcing under-allocated trajectories, NRD incorporates the adversarial sampler’s exploratory feedback into the model’s own update, greatly enhancing discovery while training a single model with no additional parameters. Our experiments support the view that these exploratory benefits can survive parameter tying, showing improved distribution learning and high-reward discovery relative to Trajectory Balance, alongside competitive performance against auxiliary exploration methods. NRD thus provides a way to exploit the adversarial formulation without maintaining a separately trained sampler.

sections.heading: A.1 Evaluation and optimization budgets
sections.text: We use seeds 39–42 and retain the prescribed final budget for each experiment, without selecting a best checkpoint. Distribution-learning curves and the structured-discovery tables report arithmetic means and sample standard deviations across these four seeds. An optimizer step in the grid and peptide comparisons counts a GFlowNet-policy update: TB, NRD, Linex, and CB contribute one per training iteration, whereas ACE, SA-GFN, and Adaptive Teacher contribute two, including their auxiliary policy. Each action moves one unit in either coordinate direction or stays in place; boundary-crossing actions are masked. Time is part of the state, so spatial revisits still define an acyclic construction process. The Rings density is the sum of two radial Gaussian kernels with radii 3 and 12, radial standard deviation 1, and a common multiplier of 10. The 8 Gaussians density sums eight isotropic Gaussian kernels of standard deviation 1, centered at equally spaced points on a circle of radius 12. sections.heading: A.4 Peptide oracle, model, and discovery protocol
sections.text: Our peptide task follows the oracle-guided sequence-design setting ( Jain et al., 2022 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) , with the alphabet and screening protocol specified here. Peptides are generated by appending amino acids or an end-of-sequence token, with maximum length ten. The alphabet contains the 19 standard amino acids other than cysteine; the end-of-sequence token also provides padding. The policy embeds each token in 32 dimensions, concatenates an eight-token context window with four sinusoidal position features, and applies one 64-unit ReLU hidden layer before the output logits. The backward transition is deterministic. The base batch is 4,096 and the constant exploration probability is 0.3. NRD, TB, CB, ACE, SA-GFN, and Adaptive Teacher use AdamW with network rate 0.05 0.05 and weight decay 0.01 0.01 ; learned log normalizers use rate 0.1 0.1 . Linex uses Adam, no weight decay, network rate 0.005 0.005 , and normalizer rate 0.02 0.02 . There is no learning-rate schedule or gradient clipping. ACE and SA-GFN collect 2,048 trajectories per branch. All methods use the same seed-specific initial principal-policy checkpoint. The oracle consists of five random-forest classifiers trained on filtered GRAMPA records ( Witten and Witten, 2019 ) , one for each of E. coli , S. aureus , P. aeruginosa , B. subtilis , and C. albicans . The preprocessing retains sequences of length one to ten, excludes cysteine and specified chemical modifications, and removes records from YADAMP. Listed peptides associated with each organism provide positive examples; an equal number of randomly generated sequences, using the empirical positive-length distribution, provide negative examples. The respective positive/negative counts per classifier are 664/664, 653/653, 396/396, 170/170, and 227/227. Classifiers use flattened one-hot sequence features, 500 trees, square-root feature subsampling, balanced class weights, and random seed 42. These models provide computational screening scores, not experimental validation of generated candidates. sections.heading: B.1 GFlowNet losses without an auxiliary exploration policy
sections.text: Trajectory Balance (TB) ( Whitammer et al., 2022 ) trains a generative policy by matching the forward trajectory flow to the terminal reward times the backward trajectory probability. Its squared log-residual penalty provides the reference update in our comparisons. Changing this penalty can change the training dynamics without changing the desired balance relation. In particular, Linex(1) ( Hu et al., 2025 ) is asymmetric: with our residual convention, its implemented penalty is exp ⁡ ( − δ ) − 1 + δ \exp(-\delta)-1+\delta . Negative residuals therefore receive different weights from equally large positive ones. This is distinct from NRD, which retains the TB semi-gradient and adds a detached, negative-residual score correction to the policy update. Contrastive Balance ( da Silva et al., 2024 ) compares trajectory log-ratios pairwise. The evaluated implementation minimizes squared differences between paired TB residuals, so the shared log-normalizer cancels. Like TB and Linex, it does not train a separate exploration policy. These comparisons distinguish a change in the balance loss from the additional sampling-distribution pressure in NRD; they do not exhaust all possible losses or their hyperparameter settings. Correctness of a balance relation at its solution is also separate from finite-budget coverage: a full-support policy can assign practically negligible probability to important regions long before it reaches that solution.

sections.heading: B.2 Methods with an auxiliary exploration policy
sections.text: ACE ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) couples a canonical GFlowNet with an exploration GFlowNet in what its authors describe as a cooperative two-player game: the explorer samples proportionally to the reward in regions under-allocated by the canonical GFlowNet, which is trained on trajectories from both policies. Its two-player structure is especially relevant here: NRD investigates whether an exploration-inducing update can be retained after identifying sampler and learner parameters. ACE instead maintains the additional sampler throughout training. The comparison tests the practical effect of this distinction, not an equivalence between their finite-step implementations. SA-GFN ( Madan et al., 2025 ) augments the principal GFlowNet with a sibling policy that uses an intrinsic novelty signal. In the evaluated implementation, random-network-distillation prediction error supplies this signal, and the principal policy learns from sibling-generated trajectories as well as its own. This adds both a policy and a learned novelty predictor. Adaptive Teacher ( Kim et al., 2025 ) instead constructs a teacher reward from the student’s trajectory-balance discrepancy and the task reward, emphasizing trajectories on which the student needs improvement. The teacher and student are optimized separately. Both approaches make exploration adaptive, but they require learned components beyond the principal policy, unlike NRD.

They are trained by minimizing balance errors over sampled trajectories, which inherently ties correctness to exploration: if a region is not visited, balance cannot be enforced there. Adaptive exploration is therefore crucial, yet standard training relies on a semi-gradient update that treats the sampling distribution as fixed at each optimization step. On the other hand, the full gradient reveals a second mechanism that reduces the observed errors in an anti-exploratory manner. In this paper, we establish a connection between the full gradient and min-min dynamics between the GFlowNet and a decoupled sampler, showing that the sampler reduces observed violations by avoiding high-error regions. This insight motivates a bridge between two-player games and single-policy dynamics, which underpins the design of our proposed method, Negative Reinforce Dynamics (NRD). By tying the parameters of an adversarial game together, we recover a single-policy dynamic that extends exploration while maintaining correctness. In standard benchmarks, our method outperforms existing approaches in both convergence speed and exploration efficiency, without training a separate teacher or auxiliary exploration policy. 1 Introduction Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn stochastic policies that construct structured objects with probability proportional to a nonnegative reward ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ) . Their ability to generate diverse high-reward samples has made them useful in applications ranging from biological sequence design ( Jain et al., 2022 ) and Bayesian structure learning ( Deleu et al., 2023 ) to recent approaches for language-model post-training ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Bartoldson et al., 2025 ) . Training a GFlowNet to sample from the target distribution is formulated by enforcing balance conditions, with correctness holding if and only if balance is satisfied globally ( Bengio et al., 2023 ) . During training, however, balance can only be corrected on trajectories that are observed, leaving poorly visited regions potentially uncorrected ( Madan et al., 2025 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026b ) . To mitigate this problem, training trajectories are often collected from an exploratory sampler, such as an ε \varepsilon -greedy policy, in order to broaden coverage ( Whitammer et al., 2022 ) . Previous work has furthermore introduced exploration mechanisms that use auxiliary samplers or teacher policies to expose the GFlowNet to regions where balance errors remain large ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) . In this paper we opt for a different path, revisiting how we solve the balance conditions in GFlowNet training. In the usual training pipeline, balance is enforced by turning local violations into a loss and minimizing its expectation over a sampling policy. However, with an adaptive sampling distribution that evolves during training, decreasing this expected loss may not correspond to correcting the underlying violations: if the policy adapts to avoid high-loss regions, then we will reduce the expected loss while retaining significant balance violations. (1) This reveals two mechanisms for decreasing the loss: one which corrects balance violations (the semi-gradient term) and one which avoids high-loss regions (the score term). Standard GFlowNet training keeps only the former by using a semi-gradient , which holds the sampling distribution fixed in the gradient computation even when that distribution depends on θ 	heta . The second term reveals an additional mechanism through which the sampling distribution can reduce the expected loss, which, under ordinary minimization, lowers the objective without enforcing balance – which is generally undesirable. Nevertheless, we ask whether this mechanism can instead be turned into a beneficial exploration signal. To do so, we reframe the full-gradient dynamics encapsulated in Equation 1 as a ‘weight-tied’ version of a cooperative two-player game between the GFlowNet and the sampling policy, and argue that it is this cooperation that leads to the harmful score term. To rectify this we formulate a second game, this time adversarial , which yields a novel beneficial exploration mechanism. By appropriately tying the two players’ weights we obtain our proposed scheme, Negative Reinforce Dynamics (NRD) , which we find to perform significantly better than standard trajectory balance training, at little additional cost. We establish theoretical guarantees for these dynamics in tractable population models. In the free-trajectory setting, NRD converges globally to the balanced solution and admits a pointwise log-ratio discrepancy comparison with semi-gradient Trajectory Balance. In one-dimensional exponential families under fast normalization, NRD reaches any positive Jeffreys-divergence threshold sooner from a common initialization, with an unbounded additive advantage in the two-trajectory setting. Finally, we evaluate NRD across multimodal distribution-matching and structured-generation tasks. The method improves convergence to target distributions and finite-budget exploration relative to standard Trajectory Balance and comparable-cost baselines, while remaining competitive with approaches that train auxiliary exploration policies. Despite its two-player motivation, NRD requires only a sign-selective score correction, applied only to trajectories with negative residuals, on top of the standard Trajectory Balance update and does not require a separately trained sampler. The first changes the training objective while keeping a single policy; the second learns an additional mechanism that redirects sampling toward regions the GFlowNet has not yet learned. Within the first direction, Linex(1) ( Hu et al., 2025 ) replaces the squared residual with a zero-avoiding loss designed to encourage exploration and sample diversity, and f f -Trajectory Balance ( Fawkes and Hartford, 2026 ) generalizes this loss design to the family of f f -divergences. Contrastive Balance ( da Silva et al., 2024 ) compares the residuals of pairs of trajectories so that the partition function cancels. With a closely related objective, Stable-GFlowNet ( Kwon et al., 2026 ) links mode collapse to the variance of the estimated normalizer and shows that removing it yields more diverse samples. In the second direction, ACE ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026a ) sets up a cooperative two-player game in which an exploration GFlowNet samples proportionally to the reward in regions under-allocated by the canonical GFlowNet. SA-GFN ( Madan et al., 2025 ) trains a sibling GFlowNet whose reward combines the task reward with a novelty bonus, and Adaptive Teacher ( Kim et al., 2025 ) trains a teacher GFlowNet rewarded by the student’s loss and the task reward, steering the student toward high-error regions. Boosted GFlowNets ( Dall’Antonia et al., 2026b ) train a sequence of GFlowNets, each fitting the reward not yet captured by its predecessors. These methods make exploration adaptive, but at the cost of training and maintaining models beyond the principal policy, along with additional hyperparameters such as allocation thresholds and reward exponents. NRD combines features of both directions. Like the methods in the first, it trains a single policy without auxiliary models and introduces no hyperparameters beyond those of Trajectory Balance; like those in the second, it includes an explicit mechanism that directs training toward unresolved balance violations. This mechanism, however, is obtained from the policy’s own score term rather than from a separately learned sampler or teacher, and it does not arise from a choice of loss. Although we analyze and evaluate NRD with Trajectory Balance, the same construction could in principle be applied on top of other balance losses. 8 Conclusion We introduced Negative Reinforce Dynamics, a novel GFlowNet training scheme that arises as a ‘weight-tied’ version of an adversarial game between the GFlowNet and a trajectory sampler.
